subject: Rodriguez v. United States (2015) and the rule that a traffic stop may not be prolonged beyond its 'mission' — how long the police can hold you at the roadside
central_question: Once the police finish a traffic stop — the ticket written, your papers handed back — can they keep you sitting there a few more minutes to walk a drug dog around your car, or does the Fourth Amendment put a limit not on where they can search, but on how long they can hold you?
viewer_promise: By the end, the viewer understands the exact moment a lawful traffic stop turns into an unlawful seizure: when the tasks tied to the traffic violation are done, the clock stops, and holding you any longer needs its own justification — the 'mission' rule the Supreme Court set in 2015.
surprise: Everything the officer did was individually legal — the stop, the license check, even a dog sniff, which by itself is not a search — yet the Court still ruled 6-3 that the stop was unconstitutional, because after the written warning he held the driver seven or eight extra minutes with no traffic-stop work left to do.
stakes: Whether the Constitution measures a seizure by the space the government invades or by the time it takes from you, and how a seven-minute roadside delay in Nebraska now governs millions of ordinary traffic stops every year.
target_audience: English-speaking US general audience interested in law, policing, privacy, civil rights and how legal systems actually work
demand_evidence: 'How long can the police detain you at a traffic stop' and 'know your rights' content is a large, durable YouTube genre; Rodriguez is the controlling Supreme Court answer.
Landmark-case explainers sustain long-tail search interest, and the traffic-stop-duration question recurs in every new roadside-detention and dog-sniff dispute.
competition: Most existing videos recite the holding or fold Rodriguez into a general Fourth Amendment survey; few center the neutral 'the case is about time, not space' causal angle and pair it with the home/person/time series arc.
differentiation: Frames Rodriguez as the finale of a three-part arc (home, person, time): the Court drew its line not around a place or a person but around the clock. Present-tense, self-relevant, primary-source cited, neutral and advertiser-safe.
research_feasibility: High: the opinion is public domain (575 U.S. 348); Cornell LII, Justia and Oyez provide the full opinion, syllabus, dissents and case record.
visual_feasibility: High: a lonely midnight highway shoulder, cold headlights, restrained reflected patrol light, a stopwatch/clock motif, a procedural K-9 silhouette, a 6-3 split, and an open-road ending — all symbolic reconstruction, no real-person likeness.
risk_notes: Decided landmark case (2015); opinion is public domain - advertiser-friendly.
Drug-adjacent subject: the methamphetamine is treated only as 'what the search found' on the court record; no drug depiction, no how-to, no glamorization.

Dennys Rodriguez and Officer Morgan Struble are real people on the public court record; treat respectfully, factually, by role; no real-person likeness in AI visuals (invariant 11). The K-9 is procedural, never depicted attacking.

Keep tone neutral between the driver's time/liberty and legitimate law-enforcement need. Do NOT overstate the holding: the Court did NOT ban dog sniffs or traffic stops; it barred prolonging a stop past its mission without reasonable suspicion, and remanded.
Restrained red-and-blue patrol light only as motivated light; never a full-screen wash or strobe. Generated visuals are reconstruction, never presented as authentic dashcam or archival footage.
kill_conditions: Cannot source the holding and key facts to the primary opinion (575 U.S. 348) plus one independent authoritative reference.
